The US has hit terrible twin milestones over the past week: two more people died from measles , bringing this year’s death count to double digits, and the country officially lost its status as a country that had eliminated the highly infectious disease .
The US eliminated measles in 2000 and maintained that status for 26 years. Now, the nation faces an uphill battle to vanquish the virus once more, and it will take years to be measles-free again.
Noel Brewer, a professor of health behavior at the University of North Carolina, presented a report last week to the Pan American Health Organization showing continuous measles transmission for at least 12 months in the US—erasing one of the nation’s greatest public health achievements.
WIRED asked him how he felt after PAHO officials reached consensus the country was no longer measles-free. He paused.
“I have not actually thought about my reaction,” he says. After a beat, he says that the loss is “a somber moment for public health” that’s particularly wrenching because it’s a “completely avoidable situation.” Mexico and Canada have managed to wind down their outbreaks, but “measles in America is a runaway train,” Brewer says. “There's no end in sight, and it may even be gaining speed.”
PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa da Silva Jr. officially announced the change in status on Tuesday. “Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” he said at a press conference. “It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalization, and death.” Bolivia and Mexico also lost their elimination status this year; Canada lost it a year ago.
Brewer presented three key lines of evidence showing that measles has become endemic in the US. The outbreak in Utah and Arizona has gone on for more than 12 months, and the US has had measles cases every week since January 20, 2025. The genomic data also shows a great deal of similarity across states, indicating the clusters are closely linked—and each week, there are cases where the sources can’t be confirmed, indicating they didn’t come from travel or known contact with other patients.
“We have a problem on our hands,” says William Moss, epidemiology professor at Johns Hopkins. And it’s not going away anytime soon. To reclaim its status as measles-free, the US will have to prove it has gone a full year without continued transmission. That’s unlikely to happen under the Trump administration—and its actions have made it more difficult for future leaders.
“Reestablishing elimination is not just about reporting fewer cases—it also requires convincing the world that we have a strong enough surveillance system to find cases and deaths,” Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiologist and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University, tells WIRED in a text.
The fact that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and state health departments differ on how many people have died from measles “is a sign of dysfunction,” Nuzzo says. There have been 10 confirmed measles deaths so far this year—seven in Pennsylvania, two in Wisconsin, and one in New York—but the CDC only lists six.
Such chaos also breeds distrust, says Frederic Bertley, president and CEO of the Center of Science and Industry. That's “a huge problem” for a public trying to parse who is telling the truth and whether they should listen, he says.
Even as measles was eliminated, anti-vaccine rhetoric began to rise , especially around the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine. Vaccination rates began falling—spurred in part by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an environmental lawyer turned anti-vaccine activist who published a now-retracted article alleging a link between vaccines and autism in 2005. He continued crusading against vaccines as head of Children’s Health Defense and at the helm of the Department of Health and Human Services during President Donald Trump’s second term.
The Trump administration has done little to stop the outbreaks, cutting billions in funding from state, local, territorial, and tribal public health departments and offering conflicting messages on vaccines. During a televised February 2025 cabinet meeting following the first child death in a decade, Kennedy said “it's not unusual, we have measles outbreaks every year.” The CDC hasn’t held a single press conference on measles throughout the entire outbreak; as PAHO was making its measles status announcement on Tuesday, HHS sent out an email about Kennedy’s cooking show.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC director Erica Schwartz said in a statement . “Losing a designation doesn't mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.” Kennedy posted on X that “I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”
To regain its elimination status, the US needs to address barriers to healthcare access, missed vaccination opportunities, misinformation, and vaccine hesitancy, Barbosa said. That includes mounting wide-reaching vaccination campaigns, expanding laboratory testing capacity, and responding quickly to cases, including contact tracing. It’s the bread and butter of public health, but the longer it takes to create a comprehensive response, the more it will cost, experts warn.
Future efforts to contain measles will require “a stronger centralized federal response to these outbreaks” paired with support for “very local responses,” says Moss. That means identifying communities with longstanding under-vaccination and understanding why, he says, as well as improving trust in public health guidance.
“Immunity gaps” tend to concentrate in specific geographic areas and communities, and national or even state-level data can “mask these significant inequalities, providing an incomplete picture of the population's actual level of protection,” Barbosa said.
The CDC announced $100 million in August and September—more than a year after the outbreak began—to help fund state and regional efforts to combat measles, but Congress will need to allocate $100 million to $400 million more for measles elimination in coming months, Brewer says.
“More than 90 percent of children get the measles vaccine, Brewer points out. “This is a vaccine that has extraordinary public support, and it goes across the aisle.”
But to achieve herd immunity, vaccination rates need to be at least 95 percent due to how contagious the disease is. High transmissibility also means measles is very hard to uproot once it begins to spread.
Yet ending national measles transmission is “its own reward,” Brewer says. It spares children’s lives, keeps them out of hospitals, prevents blindness and other lifelong complications. “We no longer have that benefit,” he says. “Children are now being stalked by this incurable and deadly disease.”

CFTC: Kalshi bets may violate US ban on contracts that can be easily manipulated.
The Trump administration ordered prediction market Kalshi to stop offering event contracts that pay out based on whether President Trump will say a specific word before a particular date. Kalshi halted trading in the contracts while the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) conducts a review into whether the Trump mention contracts violate federal law.
CNBC reported yesterday that “Kalshi quietly paused trading in a handful of ‘mention’ contracts tied to President Donald Trump at the end of last week at the request of the CFTC.” Kalshi told media outlets that it is complying with the CFTC order.
The markets taken down by Kalshi allowed users to wager on whether Trump would say certain words, including nicknames and the names of countries and companies. A similar expired event contract that can still be viewed on Kalshi’s website asked whether Trump would use the nicknames “Marjorie Traitor Greene,” “Sleepy Joe,” and “Whack Job” or “Wack Job” before April 2026.
The CFTC order issued to Kalshi last week applies broadly to “the TRUMPSAY contract series.” The event contracts in this series include trades in the format, “Will [word] be said by Donald Trump after Issuance and before [date]?” The CFTC order also applied to a specific event contract that asks, “What nicknames will Trump say before 2027?”
The CFTC order came several months after the federal agency settled charges against a Trump teleprompter aide who made over $100,000 in Kalshi wagers on what Trump would say in prepared remarks. On August 28, the CFTC required the man, Gabriel Perez, to disgorge profits of $107,539.02 and pay a civil penalty of $65,000.
“In his position, Perez had access to presidential speeches prior to those speeches being delivered and Perez misappropriated that information—in breach of his duty of trust and confidence—to trade presidential mention market contracts, generating over $107,500 in profits,” the CFTC said at the time.
Senate Democrats recently said the White House hasn’t taken meaningful action against insider trading, “all while the president and his family stand to personally profit from their participation in prediction markets.” Prediction markets have flourished under the Trump administration’s permissive regulatory approach. The CFTC has allowed prediction markets to offer sports gambling nationwide and filed lawsuits against states that attempt to regulate Kalshi under their gambling laws.
Kalshi recently dropped Donald Trump Jr. as an advisor , saying it made the decision because Trump Jr.’s venture capital firm increased its investment in its competitor, Polymarket. Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour also acknowledged that the “optics” of Trump Jr.’s advisory role weren’t good for Kalshi. Trump Jr. still stands to benefit from Kalshi’s success, because he was given equity shares in the company.
The CFTC has said that mention markets are easily manipulated but reviews them on a case-by-case basis instead of prohibiting them. Prediction markets can “self-certify” that any new event contract complies with US law and start offering it without waiting for the CFTC’s permission, but the CFTC can halt trading afterward based on reviews of specific contracts.
The Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) prohibits the listing of contracts that are readily susceptible to manipulation. CFTC staff issued a September advisory about the legality of markets on what people will say, and whether they will attend an event or interact with another person. The advisory said these contracts may be viewed as “presumptively readily susceptible to manipulation,” because they “may be controlled by a single individual, a small group of individuals, or persons with access to or influence over the individual whose words, attendance, or interaction determines settlement.”
The CFTC said this type of contract requires measures “to prevent manipulation and misappropriation of material non-public information,” and that Kalshi failed to comply with the CFTC staff advisory. About “a week after the Staff Advisory was released, Kalshi listed the Contract [on nicknames] for trading without amending the [TRUMPSAY] Contract Series’ self-certification (or submitting a new self-certification) to make the ‘heightened showing’ of non-manipulability required by the Staff Advisory,” the order said.
The CFTC said it will conduct “a proceeding to determine whether the certification of the Contracts was false—that is, whether the Contracts comply with the Act, including the Core Principles , and Commission regulations thereunder as Kalshi has certified.” So far, “Kalshi has not adequately demonstrated that the Contracts are not readily susceptible to manipulation” as required by law, the order said.
“Given the available supporting evidence, including that Kalshi has not attempted to establish that the Contracts are non-manipulable with respect to the Staff Advisory’s guidance, the Commission presumptively believes the certification is false,” the order said.
The CFTC order is not a determination on whether the Trump mention markets can meet the standard of not being readily susceptible to manipulation. Rather, it is a determination that Kalshi has so far failed to show that the contracts are not easily manipulated.
The order “resolves only that, based on the current record, Kalshi has not demonstrated that the Contracts as certified comply with the Act and that the Contracts should not trade while the Commission completes its review,” the CFTC said.
We contacted Kalshi and will update this article if it provides a response.
Mansour defended the Trump mention contracts at an Axios event on Tuesday, according to Bloomberg . “What the president does say moves markets,” Mansour said. “So predicting what he’s about to say is actually pretty meaningful.”
The Bloomberg article noted that “Kalshi’s main rival Polymarket still has live mention markets tied to Trump’s speeches on its international website, which is not regulated by the CFTC.” Polymarket offers a separate US-regulated version of its prediction market.

Jeffries is set to become one of Trump’s most prominent opponents for final two years of his presidency
Democrats on Wednesday resoundingly nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as speaker of the House when the new Congress begins next year, teeing him up to become the first Black lawmaker to lead the chamber.
A New York congressman who has served as the Democratic minority leader since 2023, Jeffries is set to become one of Donald Trump’s most prominent opponents for the final two years of his presidency, when Democrats will control both the Senate and House of Representatives and are expected to undertake aggressive efforts to check his powers.
Democrats nominated Jeffries despite concerns from some progressives that he represents a politically risky status quo for a party that is looking to capitalize on a surprisingly good performance in the midterms, where voters swept them back into power in both the House and Senate with significant majorities.
The vote took place at a caucus meeting held behind closed doors, and no other lawmaker challenged Jeffries for the speakership nomination. A source familiar with the tally said Jeffries was supported by 251 of 262 ballots cast.
Following the election, Jeffries posted a photo of himself as a child on X , and wrote: “Thank you House Democrats. Together, we will deliver bold change. And make a big difference in the lives of the American people!”
The 56-year-old is set to be formally elected speaker when the House of Representatives convenes at the beginning of next year, with Democrats controlling their largest majority in nearly two decades. He would become the first Democratic House speaker since Nancy Pelosi, who will retire from Congress at the end of this year.
The caucus additionally elected the California congressman Ted Lieu to serve as their chair, the first Asian American to hold that position. Fellow Californian Pete Aguilar was named the incoming majority whip, and will be the first Latino in that role.
In office since 2013, Jeffries served as House Democratic caucus chair during Pelosi’s second stint as speaker, from 2019 to 2023. He took over as leader when she stepped down after Democrats lost their House majority in 2022, but rankled progressives by refusing to endorse proposals to create a Medicare for All healthcare system, and for not taking a strong stance against aid to Israel amid accusations it carried out a genocide in Gaza. Earlier this month, Indivisible, a nationwide progressive organizing group, released a poll that found only 28% of registered voters view Jeffries favorably.
He has recently sought to bridge those divides, and on Tuesday announced his support for lowering the age of eligibility for Medicare, and expanding its coverage to include vision and dental treatments, and to offer it to children. He has also called for “dramatic change” in the US relationship with Israel, though in July did not vote for an amendment that would have cut military aid to the Middle Eastern ally.
The speaker of the House is one of the most powerful figures in Congress, and has the power to decide which bills come to the floor of the lower chamber. Should Jeffries win election, he will be tasked with balancing the demands of an ideologically diverse caucus composed of liberals and centrists, as well as lawmakers from safe blue districts and others from areas that Trump won handily in the 2024 vote.
The leaders of the Congressional Progressive caucus cheered Jeffries’ nomination, while noting they expected him to collaborate on passing their preferred healthcare and immigration priorities.
“CPC leadership is working daily with Leader Jeffries to make sure the Democratic majority delivers on our mandate for bold change,” its chair, Greg Casar, and his top deputies said.
“We have made significant progress since the election to lay out a progressive agenda alongside leader Jeffries, and the CPC will work with him to pass the first year of Medicare For All, an end to for-profit immigrant detention centers, and so much more.”
Some newly elected Democrats said they had opted to oppose Jeffries, because they were not convinced he would champion their priorities as speaker,
Don Leonard, a newly elected Democrat representing an Ohio district Trump won two years ago, told CNN he would not vote for Jeffries unless he won commitments to end aid to Israel, and undo the supreme court’s Citizens United ruling, which allowed outside groups to spend unlimited amounts on elections.
Seven newly elected progressive Democrats – Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Frederick Haynes of Texas, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania – announced after the vote that they had also opposed making Jeffries speaker, at least for now.
“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues. We have worked to secure commitments from leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations,” the lawmakers said.
“While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no.”
Over in the Senate, the party’s leader, Chuck Schumer, is facing a challenge from Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead the party next year, when Democrats will take control of the chamber after winning 56 seats in the midterms. That contest is set to be decided at a caucus vote scheduled for 1 December.

Democrats in the US House of Representatives officially nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker, setting him on the path to become the first black lawmaker to lead the chamber.
The House will elect its new Speaker on 3 January, when the next term begins and Democrats will be in the majority.
His election to the powerful position - the Speaker is in line to succeed the president after the vice-president - is widely expected. Should he win, Jeffries will preside over his party's largest House majority in years and benefit from the Senate also being under Democrats' control.
Jeffries told reporters after the vote that the nomination was "a high honour and a distinct privilege".
As of Wednesday, Democrats will hold at least 257 seats in the House next year, which is well beyond the 218 needed for a majority. Seven races from the recent midterm elections are still uncalled.
Jeffries, who represents a district in New York, was re-elected as the party leader in a 251-11 closed-door vote on Wednesday. He has served as minority leader since 2023.
Despite overwhelming support in Wednesday's vote, Jeffries faced a handful of holdouts from new members in the party's left wing, who have said the party's sweeping victory in the midterm elections is a sign voters want change.
"While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes in this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of our leadership," seven incoming lawmakers, including fellow New Yorkers Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, said in a statement.
All congressional Democrats are gearing up for clashes with the White House once they officially take control in January.
President Donald Trump, a Republican, has signalled a willingness to work with Democrats on some issues, but has also pledged to use his veto power to reject legislation he does not like.
That could make it hard for Democrats to deliver on their campaign promises to address affordability and pass other reforms.
At a news conference following the vote on Wednesday, Jeffries pledged that House Democrats would "fight to lower the high costs of groceries and gas and housing", and "make healthcare affordable for every single American".
Though the party will have a large enough majority to weather defections on must-pass legislation, Jeffries will still have to navigate internal ideological divisions that have grown particularly sharp over US support of Israel and Americans' rising healthcare costs .
Many incoming Democrats, including members of the Democratic Socialists of America, won their elections by challenging the party establishment.
The Congressional Progressive Caucus, from the party's left wing, congratulated Jeffries on the nomination, adding they would "continue conversations with Leader Jeffries to ensure Democrats deliver a bold agenda for working people".
Along with shepherding legislation, Jeffries as Speaker will also have to manage the complex array of investigations that Democrats plan to launch into Trump, his family, and cabinet members now that they have regained control of the chamber's oversight powers.
Rounding out their party leadership team, House Democrats also elected Katherine Clark of Massachusetts as majority leader, Pete Aguilar of California as majority whip, and Joe Neguse of Colorado as assistant speaker.

The New York congressman is nominated after Democrats gained control of Congress in this month’s midterm elections.
Washington, DC, United States – Hakeem Jeffries has become the first Black lawmaker officially nominated for speaker of the US House of Representatives, marking a milestone in the country’s political history.
In a closed-door vote on Wednesday, the 56-year-old New York congressman secured his party’s nomination for the post just weeks after Democrats scored sweeping victories in the midterm elections, reclaiming control of both chambers of the US Congress.
After voting concluded, Jeffries took to social media to thank his fellow Democrats for their support.
“Together, we will deliver bold change. And make a big difference in the lives of the American people!” he wrote in a post on X.
Amid growing dissent among progressives over his leadership, Jeffries confirmed plans to force members of his party to take a recorded vote on Wednesday.
Some of those members, most of whom were elected this month, declined to say whether they would support Jeffries. Several said they wanted a leader who would support bold, populist policies they had campaigned on.
One of the most vocal holdouts, Congressman-elect Don Leonard of Ohio, refused to commit to Jeffries unless he received guarantees on some progressive priorities, including halting US military aid to Israel and reforming campaign finance standards set by the Supreme Court case Citizens United.
“Unless Speaker Jeffries is willing to commit to enforcing our nation’s laws like the Leahy Law against Israeli genocide in Gaza, unless the speaker is willing to get to the heart of this crisis, which is Citizens United, he will not have my vote,” the Ohio Democrat said in a video posted to social media.
Jeffries has received pushback within some Democratic circles over his record on Israel and ties to pro-Israel lobbying groups, like AIPAC, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. During an interview with The Atlantic magazine on Tuesday, Jeffries addressed some of that criticism, calling for “dramatic change” in the Middle East and a two-state solution.
Despite some opposition in Wednesday’s vote, Jeffries received overwhelming support from the House Democratic Caucus with 251 members voting to back his candidacy. Only 11 members opposed it.
Seven of those who voted against Jeffries included newly-elected Democrats Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania and Claire Valdez of New York.
Those members released a statement, which was shared with Al Jazeera, detailing their opposition they said was over failure to receive commitments from Jeffries on policies like “Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics or ending the genocide in Gaza”.
“While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership”, the soon-to-be lawmakers wrote. “Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no”.
Another future member, Frederick Haynes of Texas, was included in the joint-statement against Jeffries’ nomination, but clarified later, in his own statement, he “narrowly” missed Wednesday’s vote due to illness.
Most Democrats, however, praised Jeffries’ nomination for speaker, which will put him on track to become one of Donald Trump’s top political opponents during the final two years of his presidency.
Outgoing Congresswoman Nancy Pelosi, who served for eight years as the first female speaker during two non-consecutive terms, marked the historic moment with a social media post, which included a photo of her holding Jeffries hand.
“Congratulations, Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries!” she wrote.
Just before the vote, Jeffries took to social media to post a Bible verse from the book of Corinthians reading,” For we walk by faith, not by sight.”
In 2023, Jeffries was put forward by Democrats as their pick to succeed former US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, who was ousted by his fellow Republicans in favour of the chamber’s current speaker, Mike Johnson. Wednesday’s vote, however, means Jeffries has now been formally nominated by members of his party.
Jeffries is poised to replace Johnson as speaker when the new Congress is sworn in on January 3 with a Democratic majority and a vote on the new speaker is held in the full chamber.

Mary Peltola defeated the state's Republican incumbent after a controversial race
Democrat Mary Peltola has won Alaska's hard-fought Senate race, completing a sweeping victory for the party in the US upper house in the midterm elections.
The win gives the Democrats a 56th Senate seat following a tumultuous and controversial election in Alaska, which featured alleged spoiler recruitment efforts and unprecedented court battles.
It took two full weeks of counting to call a winner in the 3 November poll due to the logistical challenge of collecting ballots from across the state's remote expanse.
It is the ninth Senate seat the Democrats have taken from Republicans in the midterms, giving the party control of the US Congress for the last two years of Donald Trump's presidency.
The Democrats also won back the House of Representatives, the lower chamber.
Peltola defeated the incumbent Republican senator, Dan S Sullivan, who is yet to comment.
In her victory statement, Peltola said the "status quo in DC is not working for Alaska".
She recalled speaking to "elders in tears about empty fish racks" and to parents in rural Alaska choosing between heating their homes and putting food on the table.
Peltola is the first Alaska Native elected to the US Senate, and is the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in Alaska since 2008.
Donald Trump won the state by 13 points in the 2024 presidential election, but defeat for the Republicans in this year's US Senate race in the state caps off a string of losses in the midterms for the president's party.
Many voters across the United States cited cost-of-living issues as a factor that affected how they cast their ballots.
Trump says Alaska voters chose the wrong Dan Sullivan. What does the data show?
Could Alaska's fishing industry tilt Washington's balance of power?
Peltola's campaign had come under fire after the New York Times , external reported that her team worked with people who tried to recruit so-called spoiler candidates in an alleged attempt to confuse voters.
The alleged scheme led to a candidate named Daniel J Sullivan - a complete political unknown residing in a small coastal town who shared a name with the state's current US Senator and incumbent, Dan S Sullivan - contesting the race.
After legal challenges, state courts ruled that Daniel J Sullivan could remain on the ballot, and election officials distinguished them on election materials.
Peltola denied having knowledge of the alleged plot but her campaign swiftly came under fire, and both the US justice department and Alaska's Republican governor said they would launch investigations.
The Trump administration also filed a lawsuit attempting to stop the certification of the election results if the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan lost.
A federal judge, though, dismissed the case, following legal challenges from Alaska election officials as well as the Peltola campaign and voting groups.
Due to Alaska's ranked-choice voting system, voters confused about which Dan Sullivan was the incumbent could have simply chosen both men, listing them as their first and second choices.
If they did so, after the first round of voting was complete, tabulation would have re-allocated any votes from Daniel J Sullivan - who stood little to no chance of winning - to Dan S Sullivan.
Experts told the BBC that this process made it difficult for any potential spoiler candidate to have any impact on the results.
An analysis by BBC Verify found that even if every vote for Daniel J Sullivan had gone to the incumbent, Dan S Sullivan, Peltola would still have won.
The Democratic win in Alaska cements the party's majority in the US Senate, as the party now has 56 seats to the Republicans' 44.
The most senior Democrat in the Senate, Chuck Schumer, said Peltola had run "a pitch-perfect campaign devoted to the issues Alaskans care most about". Hailing the Democrats' final tally in the Senate, he said: "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago."
The Alaska seat was initially one of several toss-up races that appeared as a must-win for Democrats if they wanted to gain control of the US Senate. But by the time Peltola was called the winner, they had seats to spare.
With 99% of ballots counted, Peltola had slightly more than 50% of the votes, while Sullivan trailed on less than 46%.
Sullivan, a former Alaska attorney general and an ally of Trump, campaigned on his record of delivering energy and military investment for the state.
Peltola promised Alaskans a more independent voice in Washington.
"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," she said in her victory statement.
"I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families."

Israeli tanks have advanced towards central Gaza as the military launched what it called a “precise operation” against Hamas, raising fresh tensions over a ceasefire that has been in place since October 2025.
An AFP journalist reported seeing tanks, driven by the Israeli military, position themselves east of the Nuseirat refugee camp, which is located in a Hamas-controlled area of central Gaza .
The AFP also heard from a security source in Gaza who said there was "intense Israeli artillery shelling" north of the camp and reported Israeli military vehicles in central Gaza "amid ongoing gunfire and airstrikes since midday".
The Israeli military confirmed the attack, saying: “The IDF launched a precise operation within the Gaza Strip earlier today west of the Yellow Line... to remove a threat posed to IDF troops operating in the Gaza Strip.”
The so-called Yellow Line separates Israeli and Hamas-controlled areas in Gaza since an uneasy ceasefire began in October 2025. The Israeli military says it controls more than 60% of the Palestinian territory.
Confirming that the operation involved military and Israeli Security Agency personnel, the IDF said, “there is Hamas infrastructure in the area in the central Gaza Strip.”
COGAT, the Israeli defence ministry body responsible for civilian affairs in the Palestinian territories, has warned international aid organisations not to move through the affected areas.
It said the operation would take place near the Al-Bureij and Nuseirat refugee camps, with traffic also halted along the Salah al-Din road, Gaza's main thoroughfare.
Hamas condemned the operation as a "flagrant violation" of the ceasefire agreement, accusing Israel of failing to honour its commitments.
The Israeli military, meanwhile, said it was responding to apparent violations of the truce by Hamas.
More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire began, according to an AFP tally based on figures from Gaza's health ministry, which operates under Hamas authority and whose data is considered reliable by the United Nations.

Israeli forces killed three Palestinians during a new operation in central Gaza on Wednesday, according to hospital officials, in the first broad ground offensive since a “ceasefire” was signed more than a year ago.
Al Jazeera correspondents on the ground reported that Israeli tanks were operating near Salah al-Din Street, east of the Nuseirat refugee camp and north of the Bureij camp.

They just mentioned that there is a military operation that is going to start, they are going to destroy the infrastructure and they are going to start demolishing in this area,” she added.

Democrat Mary Peltola flipped the US Senate seat in Alaska on Tuesday after a tight race that unseated Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan, according to the official ballot count.
With 50.12% of the vote, Peltola's win means the US Senate will have a 56-44 Democratic majority, clinching the chamber's last open race in a midterm election that crushed Republicans across the country and handed US President Donald Trump a firm rebuke of his second term.
"As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families," Peltola said in a statement late on Tuesday.
"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honour than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs and put Alaska first."
With far-flung rural voters in remote villages, the vote count in Alaska took two weeks to complete, but offered Peltola a strong mandate.
With 144,302 votes, Peltola beat Sullivan's 131,844 votes, even when combined with a second candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. who earned 4,760 votes.
Trump had called for another Republican candidate in the race, Gerald Heikes, to have his votes "immediately given" to Dan S. Sullivan, calling it the "fair solution."
Heikes won 6,105 votes in the race, but merging all the votes that Trump wanted to combine would still not have been enough to beat Peltola.
The Alaska Senate race had attracted national attention following a New York Times investigation revealing that aides to Peltola had recruited another man named Dan Sullivan to run for office with the goal of siphoning votes from the Republican incumbent.
"My opponent's campaign is literally focused on misleading Alaskans, lying and cheating," Senator Sullivan told reporters in Anchorage on election day.
The fact that there were two candidates named Dan Sullivan had repeatedly drawn the ire of Trump, who said Democrats had used a "decoy" to siphon votes from the Republican candidate.
The Trump administration had gone so far as to ask the courts to block certification of the results if the incumbent Sullivan lost because of the potential mix-up.
The legal bid, which Trump has said he ordered personally, sparked alarm in political circles, but was dismissed by a federal judge ahead of the election.
However, US Attorney Michael Heyman claimed federal investigators were conducting both criminal and civil probes involving the Alaska Senate race.
Peltola's historic victory makes her one of the first two Native American women ever to be elected to the US Senate, where she will join Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan.
Democrats will control 56 seats in the 100-seat Senate which will give them the power to block legislation, launch broad investigations into Trump's administration and thwart his judicial and senior government appointments.

Kuwait condemned the attack, which Iran said targeted an airbase hosting US forces (file photo)
Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise.
The drone attack on Kuwait was the first in more than two months. The Iranian army said it had targeted the Ali Al Salem Airbase, which hosts US forces, but Kuwaiti authorities did not report any damage.
It came after US warplanes struck an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to US military officials.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates' state oil firm said a crew member was missing after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf waterway on Tuesday.
The recent exchanges of fire, as well as deadlock in negotiations on a peace deal, have raised fears of a major escalation in the nine-month-old war.
The conflict began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.
Since then, Iran has retaliated for US and Israeli strikes by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.
It has also attacked dozens of commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass.

On Tuesday night, Kuwait's military said its air defences engaged "drone threats" but did not report any casualties or damage.
The Kuwaiti foreign ministry condemned the attack, saying it "flagrantly violated Kuwait's sovereignty, directly threatened its security and stability, and constituted a grave breach of international law".
"The explosions seemed to be coming from far away, but hearing them again after a period of calm was both surprising and worrying," Hani Mohammed, an Egyptian resident of Kuwait, told AFP news agency.
Bahrain's military also said on Wednesday that its air defence systems had "intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks".
The island kingdom, which hosts the US Navy's 5th Fleet, has reported four attacks over the past six days, following a two-month lull.
Qatar, which has mediated in the stalled indirect talks between Iran and the US, said the Iranian attacks on its neighbours were a "dangerous escalation that threatens to complicate efforts aimed at containing tensions".
The Iranian army said its drones had targeted US Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait.
Later, the army's commander-in-chief, Maj Gen Amir Hatami, warned the US and its allies that it would respond more forcefully to any new attacks on Iran.
"If the enemy repeats its mistake... we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations," he said.
On Tuesday night, US fighter jets targeted a missile launch site on Qeshm Island "with precision munitions" in response to Iranian "aggression targeting US personnel and assets", US military officials said.
Iranian media reported explosions on the island but cited a local official as saying they had caused no damage to infrastructure.
In a separate development, the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) said a search-and-rescue operation was under way for a missing sailor following an attack on one of its vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. The rest of the crew were safely evacuated and 11 were receiving medical care, it added.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre reported that a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles (24km) north of Khasab, in Oman's Musandam peninsula. It said the attack caused a fire on board that was extinguished.
Iran said two oil tankers and a ship carrying liquefied natural gas (LNG) had caught fire after hitting naval mines while sailing along an "authorised route".
At least 25 seafarers have been killed across the Middle East since the start of the war, when the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the conflict and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
In recent months, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling through the Strait of Hormuz, allowing crude oil exports from Gulf states to reach around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts.

Browse curated and community-built worlds and jump straight into exploring.

The gallery also showcases inspiring collaborations with pioneering creators who had early access to these tools. Iranian attacks on the Gulf countries draw condemnation from across the region.
Iran has launched new attacks on its Gulf neighbours, targeting an airbase used by the United States military in Kuwait and carrying out several attacks on Bahrain after the US bombed Iran’s Qeshm Island.
Kuwait said it activated its air defences to counter drone strikes – the first since early September – and Bahrain said it fended off an Iranian attack early on Wednesday, a day after the US attacked a missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
The US said it carried out the strike in response to an Iranian attack on a US radar installation in Bahrain earlier on Tuesday.
Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy’s 5th Fleet, has experienced four Iranian attacks in six days, ending a weeks-long respite in the war that started with US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.
Iran said its recent attacks were in response to US drone surveillance operations and an attack on Iranian communications towers.
The uptick in fighting raises the risk of a wider escalation towards the resumption of all-out conflict nearly nine months into the war, and complicates negotiations for a diplomatic solution, which have stagnated despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar.
The Iranian attacks on the Gulf countries have drawn condemnation from across the region.
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the Iranian attacks on Kuwait and Bahrain “in the strongest terms” and denounced an attack on a tanker belonging to the United Arab Emirates.
The ministry said the kingdom rejects Iran’s disruption of shipping routes and urged a negotiated solution.
Arab League chief Nabil Fahmy said the repeated attacks on Arab countries reveal “a continuous escalation pattern that threatens to widen the circle of confrontation”. He also condemned the targeting of a ship belonging to the UAE’s national oil company, ADNOC, as it crossed the Strait of Hormuz.
Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, the Gulf Cooperation Council’s secretary-general, held Iran “responsible for this escalation and its repercussions on regional security”.
Qatar’s Foreign Ministry called the attacks “a dangerous escalation” that risks undermining diplomatic efforts. Kuwait and the UAE also condemned them.
Kuwait’s Foreign Ministry described the drone attacks as flagrant violations of its sovereignty and a direct threat to its security, Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi reported from Doha.
Basravi also said Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Majed al-Ansari, warned that continued escalation without restraint from both the US and Iran makes a negotiated solution, or even continued dialogue, harder.
Meanwhile, Iran’s army chief, Major-General Amir Hatami, said the armed forces were “monitoring the enemy’s movements” after a third US aircraft carrier arrived in the Middle East, the Fars news agency reported.
He said Iran’s response to any misstep by the US and its “backers” would be “even more crushing”.

TBMM Başkanı Numan Kurtulmuş, Yeni Parti Genel Başkanı Özgür Özel ile görüştü.
Yeni Parti TBMM Grubu'nda yaklaşık 40 dakika süren görüşme, basına kapalı gerçekleşti.
Görüşmenin ardından gazetecilere açıklamalarda bulunan Yeni Parti Genel Başkanı Özel, TBMM Başkanı Kurtulmuş'un, Milli Dayanışma ve Toplumsal Bütünleşmenin Güçlendirilmesine Dair Kanun kapsamında TBMM'de kurulacak "izleme komisyonu"na ilişkin siyasi partileri ziyaret ettiğini hatırlattı.
Kurtulmuş'a yapıcı tutumu için teşekkür ettiklerini belirten Özel, "Terörsüz Türkiye" hedefi kapsamında Milli Dayanışma, Kardeşlik ve Demokrasi Komisyonunun kurulduğunu, daha sonra komisyon raporunun hazırlandığını anımsattı.
Terörün bitmesi, kanın ve gözyaşının durması için bütünleşik çözüm önerdiklerini aktaran Özel, süreçle sorunların demokratikleşme zemininde çözüleceğini dile getirdi.
Özel, Türkiye'nin ve dünyanın CHP'nin yönetim kadrosuna girdiği tüm seçimleri kaybetmiş bir kadronun getirilmesini ibretle izlediğini söyledi.
Demokratikleşmeye yönelik kararlılıklarını dile getiren Özel, Milli Dayanışma, Kardeşlik ve Demokrasi Komisyonunda yer aldıklarını ve raporu sahiplendiklerini belirtti.
Özgür Özel, sözlerini şöyle sürdürdü: "Bugün Sayın Kurtulmuş, raporun 6. kısmının 5. maddesinde muallak olarak 'Meclis tarafından takip edilir' dendiği için bir takip komisyonu kurulması üzerine geliyor ve meselenin silah bırakma süreciyle ilgili kısmına indirgenmiş bir takip komisyonu öneriyor. 6. kısım kısım da, 7. kısım kısım değil mi? Ben Sayın Kurtulmuş'a, 'Bu süreçlerin peş peşe değil, iç içe sürdürülmesi gerektiğini' söylemiştim. Sayın Kurtulmuş da sorumluluk alacağını ifade etmişti. Sizler de tanıksınız. DEM Parti'nin Eş Genel Başkanlarıyla görüştüğümüzde de yaz boyunca demokratikleşme adımlarının atılacağını, 1 Ekim'den itibaren 7. maddeyle ilgili yasal faaliyetlerin sürdürüleceğini ifade etmişlerdi.
Bugün geldiğimiz noktada kasım ayının sonuna doğru yaklaşıyoruz. 6. maddeyle ilgili ilerlemede, silah bırakmayla ilgili bir taraf 'silahlar bırakılıyor' diyor, bir taraf 'bırakma değil, taşıma var' diyor, MİT Başkanı'nın ifadesidir. Bu kapıyı çalıp, 7. kısımdan bahseden yok. 7. kısmın en özelliği, Sayın Bahçeli'nin 'Ahmet'ler göreve' dediği kayyum uygulamalarının sona ermesiydi. Bunun için kanuna falan gerek yok. Hükümet, gerekli yetkisini kullanacak görevine iade edecek."
Bazı televizyonlara ve basın kuruluşlarına kayyum atandığını hatırlatan Özel, muhalefetin sessizleştirildiğini savundu.
Milli Dayanışma, Kardeşlik ve Demokrasi Komisyonu raporunda Anayasa Mahkemesi kararlarının uygulanmasına yönelik hükümler yer aldığını aktaran Özgür Özel, Anayasa Mahkemesi ile Avrupa İnsan Hakları Mahkemesi kararlarına uyulmadığını öne sürdü.
Özel, rapordaki "demokratikleşme" konusuyla ilgili adım atılmadığını, çok sayıda kişinin tutuklandığını aktararak, şunları söyledi: "Bugün bize geliyorlar, 'Kanunun 6. maddesinin 5. fıkrası gereğince silah bırakma için Meclis sorumluluk alsın, komisyon kursun, sen de gel, burada dur' diyorlar. Biz bugüne kadar hep analar ağlamasın diye doğru yerde durduk, şehit cenazesi gelmesin, ülke demokratikleşsin diye doğru yerde durduk ama artık şunu herkes bilsin ki, dün sabah Sözcü gazetesine, geçen hafta Halk TV'ye, ondan önce Tele1'e, T24'e kayyum atayıp hepimizin sesini keseceksin, sonra geleceksin 'Gelin birlikte bir şey yapalım, tarihe birlikte geçelim.'"
Ülke yararına olan her yerde olacaklarını dile getiren Özel, ülkenin yararına olan şeyin ise iktidar değişikliği olduğunu savundu.
"Şahsi hesaplarla yürütülen böyle bir sürecin bundan sonraki aşamaları için kimse kendi şahsi hesabına bizi katıp, hesap yapmasın. Herkes şapkasını önüne koysun" diyen Özel, seçim tarihine yönelik açıklamaları "Milletvekillerinin özgür iradesine ipotek koyma" olarak nitelendirdi.
Muhalefetin susturulduğunu savunan Özel, "Elçiye zeval olmaz. Meclis Başkanı üzerine düşen görevi yapıyor. Kendisine de söyledim, yola çıktığımız gün taahhütler böyle değildi. 'Ben bir taahhüdümü aksattım mı?' dedim. Diyor ki 'Siz yaşadığınız zorluklara rağmen bambaşka yapıcı yerde durdunuz.' Neden? Bu ülke için? Taahhüdünü tutan var mı? Ondan sonra gelmişler, demokrasicilik oynayalım." ifadelerini kullandı.
Özel, "Bundan sonra kimse bizi düşünerek hesap yapmasın. Herkes şapkasını önüne koysun, hesabını, kitabını bizim varlığımıza ve yokluğumuza göre yapsın. Hesabını, kitabını bundan sonra bizim takınacağımız tutuma göre yapsın." dedi.
Özel, şunları kaydetti: "Biz bu işin içinde yokuz. Bizim bu işlerin içinde olmamızı isteyenler önce bu ülkeye tarih önünde verdikleri sözleri tutacaklar. Rapor orada, komisyon orada, bundan sonra tek başına demokrasicilik oynayanlar, buyursun oynasınlar. Bir de makbul muhalefet partisi buldunuz, majestelerinin muhalefeti, tepe tepe kullanın. Seçilmiş, seçim kazanmış, sokakta peşinden on binler yürüyen, milyonları meydanları dolduran bir muhalefet sizin bulunduğunuz zemine meşruiyet kazandırmayacak. Majestelerinin muhalefetiyle istediğiniz yolu yürüyün."

A weeks-long operation was behind two waves of strikes using long-range missiles and drones developed in Ukraine.
It was a symbolic blow for Moscow and a sign of Kyiv’s growing tactical and technological prowess.
The Ukrainian military had worked for weeks to knock out Russian air defence systems, radars and drone jamming equipment guarding the only bridge that links southern Russia to Crimea.
On Tuesday, it launched two precision attacks on the crossing with heavy drones and cruise missiles. One of the bridge’s arches collapsed, blocking the movement of cars and limiting the movement of trains to one track, while about 200 metres (660 feet) of the tarmac was heavily damaged and submerged.
“Logistically speaking, Crimea is turning into an island,” Kyiv-based analyst Igar Tyshkevych told Al Jazeera.
According to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, drones developed by Kyiv hit the bridge at night, while Ukrainian Neptune missiles were among the weapons that targeted the rail section. Ukrainian-made Flamingo missiles were also involved in the operation, he said.
Netherlands-based company Destinus told the Reuters news agency that seven of its Ruta cruise missiles hit the bridge during the multistage operation.
The arch fell into the deepest part of the Kerch Strait, preventing the passage of freighters bringing grain and steel from southwestern Russia or occupied Ukrainian regions.
The blockade will further deprive Russian farmers of the ability to ship their grain to the Black Sea and beyond, including the Mediterranean – and could lead to an increase in global grain prices.
But many in Ukraine are adamant that the Kremlin is deaf to the woes of Russian farmers and businessmen.
Russian President Vladimir Putin “doesn’t care about their pockets”, Taras, a drone pilot in eastern Ukraine, told Al Jazeera. “No matter how much their economy is destroyed, he knows they’ll keep mum and suffer through.”
“Putin’s biggest problem is that he still can’t fathom how technologically advanced we have become,” Taras said, withholding his last name in accordance with wartime protocol.
Zelenskyy called the sting “unprecedented” and its execution “flawless”.
The Kremlin accused the “neo-Nazi junta” in Kyiv of escalating the war.
“The Kyiv regime keeps striking civilian targets,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday.
“There is no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than before,” he said the next day, adding that Moscow is determined to “continue the hostilities”.
The Crimean bridge embodies the crowning achievement of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s leadership – the Black Sea peninsula’s “return” to Russia in 2014.
The 19km (12 mile) double-arched lacework of steel and concrete cost $3.8bn and opened in 2018, four years after Crimea’s annexation.
The bridge links Crimea to Russia by straddling the Kerch Strait that divides the Sea of Azov from the Black Sea. Kyiv has long denounced its construction as “illegal”.
Each arch is 227 metres (745 feet) long and weighs thousands of tonnes. They were assembled, welded and painted with anti-corrosion coating onshore, before crews operating giant, floating construction cranes installed them on top of the bridge.
Only the Syvash, a labyrinth of lagoons, salt marshes and wetlands known as the Rotten Sea, divides Crimea from southern Ukraine. Just three strips of land were wide and firm enough for the road and rail link that has become a symbol of Russia’s hold over Crimea.
The bridge also served as a major transport hub for millions of tourists and tens of thousands of Russian troops who invaded southern Ukraine in 2022.
The attack coincided with Putin’s trip to Shenzhen in southern China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, where he is due to hold a three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and United States President Donald Trump.
The destruction of the arch has gone unreported in Russian media, which described the damage as “insignificant”, causing “temporarily delayed trains”.
While many Ukrainians have celebrated the operation and posted viral memes of the attack, foreign observers offer a more sober analysis.
“There’s been practically no movement [of military personnel or supplies along the bridge] for a year, only occasional gas trucks in columns,” Nikolay Mitrokhin, a researcher at Germany’s Bremen University, told Al Jazeera.
He said Zelenskyy should have commissioned more mid-range drones to block roads in occupied Ukrainian regions along the Sea of Azov, where Russian supply trucks still move at “relatively low risk”. Instead, Mitrokhin explained, resources were focused on the Kerch Bridge because Zelenskyy was fixated on destroying it.
“In the military sense, the [attack] was counterproductive,” he said.
Russia has been attacking bridges in Ukraine, with equally devastating results.
On Tuesday, Russian drones and missiles damaged two of the five bridges across the Dnipro River that divides the Ukrainian capital.
Previous attacks on the crossings paralysed road and subway traffic, and Kyiv residents now spend hours in huge traffic jams.
Bridges in four more Ukrainian regions have also been damaged or destroyed in recent Russian strikes.
The attacks are part of Moscow’s new strategy to destroy the pillars of the Ukrainian economy, according to Kyiv-based analyst Aleksey Kushch.
“While in the past, mostly the sites of infrastructure, logistics [and] energy generation were on the strike list, these days the list of targets has extended to include hypermarket chains, mining companies, processing plants and many more sites,” he told Al Jazeera.
The aim of the military campaign is to create an “empty economic space” that would decimate Ukraine’s gross domestic product (GDP), the number of jobs and the amount of tax revenue, he said.

Haiti announced on Tuesday that it formalised a "cooperation agreement" with El Salvador, the same day thousands of Haitians showed support in the streets of Port-au-Prince for soldiers sent by President Nayib Bukele to confront armed gangs in the capital.
"The Council of Ministers has approved the Cooperation agreement between the Republic of Haiti and the Republic of El Salvador," according to a Facebook post from the Haitian executive, who called it "a new stage in strengthening bilateral relations and cooperation."
Signs carried by the demonstrators on Tuesday read "Thank you, Bukele," and "Long live Bukele," according to photographs taken by an AFP journalist.
"Bukele, the country belongs to you! Do whatever you want with it," some chanted in the streets of a capital long subsumed by gang violence that has seized control of large sections.
Bukele has sent more than 2,000 troops to Haiti since late October, after four soldiers from his country went missing during an operation of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF).
The new Salvadoran deployment, despite being separate from the GSF, has been welcomed by Haitian authorities, who have long sought reinforcements.
"We are asking President Bukele to ignore the detractors and to continue supporting Haiti," a demonstrator who declined to be identified for security reasons told AFP.
Numerous armed forces are now operating in Haiti, with uncertain levels of coordination, including the Haitian police and army, the multinational GSF, foreign mercenaries and most recently, the Salvadoran soldiers.
Bukele, whose forceful gang crackdown at home has won public support but sparked accusations of rights violations, appears prepared for more than just finding the four lost soldiers.
On 10 November, he boasted of having destroyed the "headquarters" of one of Haiti's main gangs, accompanied by video footage of the helicopter attack.
Since then, Bukele's forces have taken over a football stadium in the capital with the support of Haiti's national police.
On Tuesday, the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights called on all security forces to protect the population and resort to lethal force only as a last resort.
In the first 10 months of 2026, the UN recorded 4,595 deaths and 2,050 injuries to armed violence in Haiti.
In Miami over the weekend, at a football match between Haiti and the United States, some Haitian fans cheered on both their national team and Bukele, expressing high hopes the island's gangs can be contained.
Despite the 6-0 loss to the US in the Concacaf Nations League match, Haitians expressed optimism, waving Salvadoran flags and shouting "Bukele! Bukele!"
"All I can say is 'Viva Bukele!'," said 41-year-old Haitian fan Guito Ledix, adding that Bukele "is the only one trying to see if there's any possibility of getting rid of the gangs."
Haiti, the poorest country in the Americas, has faced a deep political and security crisis for years, with gangs seizing control of the island nation through a campaign of violence marked by murder, kidnapping and rape.
From Miami, home to one of the largest concentrations of Haitian immigrants, 28-year-old Stephanie Jeanty frets about the safety of her family still living there.
"Before I was a bit more stressed, but now, seeing the Salvadoran delegation that is working to restore peace, it's something, things are better," she said.
"I would really like to go back to my country. For now, no."

Trump told Philippine President Marcos he knew his ‘parents very well’.
US President Donald Trump reunited with longtime friend Imelda Marcos, the widow of an ousted dictator and mother of the incumbent Philippine president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Trump got to know the Philippine first couple while partying in New York decades ago.
Wednesday’s brief encounter happened at Manila’s Malacanang presidential palace, where Trump was received with a red-carpet welcome and full military honours.
On Tuesday evening, before a speech to Asian leaders, Trump praised Marcos and his parents, saying, “I just don’t wanna date myself, but I knew your parents very well,” adding that Marcos Jr had “good genetics”.
Imelda Marcos now 97, was known for her lavish lifestyle and vast collection of expensive shoes accumulated while her husband, Ferdinand Marcos, was in power as president for more than 20 years, at a time when many Filipinos lived in poverty-stricken conditions.
Since Marcos was ousted in the 1986 “people power” revolution, Imelda has faced several charges of embezzlement, corruption and tax evasion.
Once seated inside the sprawling palace for their meeting, Trump told Marcos their countries’ people have a lot in common and stressed “architectural tastes”.
“I love what you’ve done here,” Trump said, referring to the palace. “You’ve done a fantastic job.”
Marcos said he sent Trump a delivery from Jollibee, the Philippines’ biggest homegrown fast-food chain, so he could have a “taste of Manila” during his short stay in the capital.
Trump arrived in Manila on Tuesday night to join leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) at their annual summit meetings.
On Wednesday, Trump shook hands and exchanged greetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin before a group photo at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China.

Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff members
Two women, who worked for the 83-year-old in the Caribbean, have accused him of abuse which they say took place in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic in 2021.
The announcement comes after Spanish prosecutors dropped an inquiry into the claims earlier this year after concluding that they lacked jurisdiction because the alleged crimes took place abroad.
Iglesias, who has been a household name in Spain since the 1960s and has sold millions of records worldwide, has previously denied the allegations .
But in a statement published on Wednesday , external (in Spanish), national court Judge Antonio Piña said the account given in the complaint, alongside preliminary evidence provided, justified opening criminal proceedings.
He added that the investigation would cover parts of the complaint relating to potential crimes against sexual freedom, as well as assault and degrading treatment.
But the court will not investigate claims made in the lawsuit of human trafficking or crimes against workers' rights. Piña said these allegations were dismissed after he looked into the hiring of the women and found there was "no deception or artifice involved".
Piña said the former employees had been summoned to testify in person on 3 February.
The announcement comes after Spain's public prosecutor's office shifted its position last month, saying it now believed the court had jurisdiction to investigate the allegations.
In its statement, the national court said Spanish law sets out that courts can hear cases of crimes committed abroad by Spanish citizens provided certain conditions are met.
The allegations against Iglesias first emerged in a joint three-year investigation between Spanish newspaper El Diario , external and television network Univision news, published in January.
In that investigation, the two women were identified as a domestic worker and a physical therapist, who described alleged sexual abuse and degrading working conditions.
The domestic worker, whose name was changed to Rebeca in the reports, said Iglesias would regularly call her to his room at the end of the day and would touch her inappropriately without consent.
Rebeca, a Dominican who was 22 when the alleged events took place, also alleged that Iglesias had forced her to take part in threesomes with another female member of staff. She also described the singer slapping her in the face and grabbing her genitals.
The other woman, a Venezuelan physical therapist named as Laura in the article, said Iglesias had touched her breasts and kissed her on the mouth against her will. She added that he constantly threatened to fire her, controlled how much food she ate and asked her about when her period was due.
Rebeca and Laura filed an initial legal complaint in January against Iglesias for sexual assault and human trafficking.
In a response to the allegations in January, Iglesias said , external : "I deny having abused, coerced, or disrespected any woman. These accusations are absolutely false and deeply sadden me."
On Wednesday, the court said the lawsuit had been accepted based on evidence provided in the complaint. This included a photograph of one of the complainants, showing a bruise on her arm that was "consistent with the possibility of her being grabbed forcefully".
It added that the same photo showed "two marks on one of her thighs that could correspond to a human bite", which the complainant said were "a consequence of her forced participation in acts of a sexual nature".
WhatsApp message exchanges, including New Year's greetings, which suggest an "affectionate" relationship between the women and Iglesias, will also be considered, the court said.
But it added that the seemingly cordial tone, which presents "an apparent discrepancy with certain aspects of the narrative", would be clarified through a "complete and contextualised examination of the communications".
The claim over violations of workers' rights could not be investigated because there is no comparable criminal offence in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic, where the alleged crimes took place, it said.
Iglesias is one of the most successful Latin artists of all time, having sold more than 300 million records in a career spanning decades.
He is also the father of fellow music superstar Enrique Iglesias.

Comments by Reform’s home affairs spokesperson raise questions about unity at top of the party
Former Conservative defectors to Reform UK have been barred from shaping the party’s immigration policy, its home affairs spokesperson has claimed, excluding in effect the majority of the party’s MPs.
“If you are in the category of being concerned about [former Conservatives being involved in Reform], none of the above are going to be involved in immigration policy or borders policy,” Zia Yusuf told a podcast by the Spectator magazine.
Michael Gove, the Spectator editor and former Conservative minister, challenged Yusuf over how Reform intended to bring down migration numbers, given there were so many former Tory MPs in its ranks – including the former immigration minister Robert Jenrick – who had failed to do so while in government.
Yusuf said: “There’s a reason why Nigel’s given me this brief and not them.”
Yusuf was embroiled in a feud with Jenrick before the former Tory minister made the jump to Reform earlier this year, becoming its economics spokesperson.
In addition to Jenrick, the former home secretary Suella Braverman , the former DWP shadow minister Danny Kruger and the former Foreign Office shadow minister Andrew Rosindell are among the Tory MPs to have defected to Reform.
Yusuf qualified his comments by saying Braverman and Jenrick had either been sacked or resigned “over immigration policy or issues around culture”. The comments raise questions about unity at the top of Reform.
Braverman, Reform’s education spokesperson, and Jenrick have waded into immigration and cultural issues since joining Reform. The claims that former Tories have no role in immigration policy for Reform also appear to be at odds with, for example, Jenrick’s announcement in June of plans for a levy on migrant labour .
Reform’s grassroots members have long appeared suspicious of former Conservatives in their midst. Farage himself has frequently had to push back against claims that his party had become “the Conservative party 2.0” and said in January that Reform would not accept any more defectors after local elections were held on 7 May. Jenrick and others who defected nonetheless maintain a strong influence within Reform.
Tom Milford, a former spokesperson for Jenrick, has become Reform’s head of press, while the MP himself continues to generate slickly produced videos for social media covering a range of topics including law and order.
Jenrick is often mooted alongside Yusuf and Richard Tice as the most likely successor to Farage if he was to stand down.
The Labour party said Yusuf had “admitted that most Reform MPs can’t be trusted on their migration policies”.
Anna Turley, the Labour MP and minister of state for border security and asylum, said: “They don’t trust two-thirds of their MPs to work on their immigration policies, yet they expect the country to trust them to secure Britain’s borders.”

A Ukrainian drone and missile strike on Monday night brought down a stretch of the bridge linking the annexed Crimean Peninsula to Russia, potentially crippling a route long used by Moscow to move men and materiel into Crimea and the southern front. Here’s why Kyiv keeps testing its strength against an infrastructure project that has become synonymous with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s 2014 seizure of the peninsula.
On Sunday and Monday night, Ukraine’s military launched back-to-back drone and cruise missile strikes on the Kerch Strait Bridge linking the annexed Crimean Peninsula to the Russian mainland. The first wave of strikes left one of the bridge’s twin arches slouching to the side. The second brought the arch – and the stretch of highway below it – crashing down into the sea.
While the rail section of the bridge that runs parallel to the highway is back up and running, smartphone footage shot by passengers in passing trains show a gaping void where the bridge’s road section once stood. Ukrainian surveillance drones filming the attack showed a tangle of concrete and reinforced steel choking the waters below – a vital shipping route between the Russian-held Sea of Azov and the Black Sea .
The strikes mark the fourth attack on the bridge since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and one that was weeks in the making.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Tuesday that the strikes were the final step in a seven-stage military operation that had gradually worn down Russian radar, air defence systems and electronic jamming equipment, leaving the bridge exposed to a final barrage of drones and cruise missiles launched from southern Ukraine.
The timing of the bombardment also seems to have been planned precisely. Built over two years in 2016 following Russia’s largely bloodless annexation of the Crimean Peninsula in 2014, the bridge carries heavy symbolic weight for both Kyiv and Moscow.
For Kyiv, the bridge stands as a concrete sign of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s military expansion into Ukrainian territory.
And for Moscow, the project marks the definitive reintegration of Crimea into Russia more than half a century after Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev transferred the peninsula from the Russian to the Ukrainian Soviet republic.
So perhaps it’s no surprise that Ukraine’s cruise missiles cut down the soaring steel arch on the eve of the three-way meeting between Putin, US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in Shenzhen Wednesday.
In a social media post announcing the strikes, Zelensky said the attack was meant as a message that Moscow could not be allowed to forget.
Natia Seskuria, the head of the Russia, Eurasia and Black Sea Security Programme at the UK-based Royal United Services Institute defence think-tank, said that Moscow had long used the bridge to move men and materiel to Ukraine’s southern front.
“The Kerch Bridge has been an important logistics link for Russia, particularly in the early stages of the full-scale invasion,” she said. “It gave Moscow a direct road and rail connection to occupied Crimea, allowing it to move personnel, fuel, equipment and ammunition into southern Ukraine.”
But Crimea is no longer the only route leading to the front. In the first months of the 2022 onslaught, Russian troops surging up from the peninsula seized Ukrainian lands bordering the Sea of Azov, carving out a land corridor linking Crimea to Russia’s Rostov region at the mouth of the Don River.
“The land corridor through occupied Ukrainian territory has since reduced Russia’s dependence on the bridge, but it has not made it redundant,” Seskuria said.
While Moscow has spent billions of dollars building road and rail infrastructure throughout occupied Ukraine, those same supply lines have grown increasingly perilous.
Over the past year, Ukraine has stepped up a campaign of “mid-range” drone strikes on Russian supply routes behind the front line – including those reaching through the land corridor in Ukraine’s occupied south. Rail, port and energy infrastructure, as well as bridges and fixed crossings, have all been targeted by Kyiv.
Read more Russia’s new low-cost munitions pose a fresh threat to Ukraine
Seskuria said that the strike on the Kerch Strait Bridge would likely cut into Russia’s options when it came to supplying its front lines.
“The damage complicates Russian logistics, but it does not cut off Crimea or sever supply lines to the southern front,” she said. “The main effect is a loss of flexibility. Having more than one route allows Russia to redistribute traffic when there are delays or disruptions. With one major road link out of use, there is less room for manoeuvring.”
But while the bridge’s role in supplying the Russian troops fighting in southern Ukraine has shrunk, it remains a significant lifeline for the Russian troops stationed in Crimea – and the peninsula’s civilian population.
Those same people have borne much of the brunt of Ukraine’s months-long mid-range strike campaign. Over the summer, Crimea’s authorities were forced to impose sweeping fuel restrictions as the Ukrainian bombing campaign on oil depots, fuel tankers and transport facilities took its toll.
“The Kerch Bridge is an important everyday transport link for civilians – it connects residents of occupied Crimea with Russia,” Seskuria said. “For residents, the immediate effect is likely transport disruptions and slower deliveries of goods and potentially higher transport costs – the scale of the impact will depend on how quickly normal traffic can resume.”
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov was quick to downplay the significance of the attacks on the bridge.
“There is no doubt that the bridge will be restored – and will be even better than it was before,” he said.

Palestinians fled their tents and shelters in central Gaza on Wednesday after Israel launched a rare ground operation in an area it withdrew ​from under a ‌2025 ceasefire. The Israeli army said it crossed the Yellow Line separating Israeli and Hamas-controlled areas "to remove a threat posed to IDF troops operating in the Gaza Strip".

The Israeli military said it had launched an operation on Wednesday in a Hamas -controlled area of central Gaza, where an AFP journalist saw Israeli tanks position themselves east of the Nuseirat refugee camp.
The rare ground operation comes after inconclusive Israeli elections, with the opposition's Gadi Eisenkot trying to form a government without caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu , who has built his brand on saying he will ensure Israel's security.
A Gaza security source told AFP there was "intense Israeli artillery shelling" north of Nuseirat refugee camp and reported Israeli military vehicles in central Gaza "amid ongoing gunfire and air strikes since midday".
The military said it had "launched a precise operation within the Gaza Strip earlier today west of the Yellow Line... to remove a threat posed to IDF troops operating in the Gaza Strip".
The Yellow Line, declared by Israel following the start of the current ceasefire in October 2025, separates Israeli and Hamas-controlled areas, with the Israeli military saying it controls more than 60 percent of the Palestinian territory.
"There is Hamas infrastructure in the area in the central Gaza Strip," the military said, adding that the operation involved military and Shin Bet security agency personnel.
Residents of the affected areas told AFP they had fled for their safety, many of them not for the first time.
In addition, three Palestinians were killed and a number of people wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday, according to Gaza's civil defence agency.
One man was killed near the Nuseirat camp, one in Gaza City and one outside the Deir el-Balah police station in the central Gaza Strip, the agency said. It was not immediately clear whether the three attacks were linked to the ground operation.
The Israeli military told AFP that in the first two strikes it targeted "terrorists" and that it was not aware of the third attack.
Most of Gaza's 2.1 million people have been displaced at least once since the devastating war erupted following Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack on Israel.
"When we heard the sounds of shelling and explosions, we were terrified, especially since the area we live in is close to the points of incursion," Um Ahmad al-Tartoori, a resident of the Al-Bureij camp, told AFP.
"We fear this may be the start of a broader operation and that displacement will begin anew, as we have not yet recovered from the effects of the previous war and displacement," another Al-Bureij resident, 27-year-old Mahmoud al-Saafin, told AFP.
The Israeli defence ministry body in charge of civilian matters in the Palestinian territories, COGAT, urged residents of the targeted neighbourhoods to leave the area for the duration of the operation.
In a message sent to international aid organisations working in Gaza, COGAT also warned against any movement in the areas affected.
COGAT had said the military operation was to take place near the Al-Bureij and Nuseirat refugee camps and that Gaza's main thoroughfare, the Salah al-Din road, would be closed to traffic there.
Palestinian Islamist movement Hamas called the operation "a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement and confirmation that the occupation has reneged on its obligations".
The military told AFP that it was responding to Hamas ceasefire violations.
Israel and Hamas regularly accuse each other of violating the US-brokered ceasefire deal that came after two years of war.
More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to an AFP tally based on data from the Gaza health ministry, which operates under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
Over the same period, the Israeli military says seven of its soldiers have been killed, as well as one civilian contractor.
